The maximum volume is

\[
\boxed{\frac{9\sqrt{21}}{7^3\,2^{14}}}.
\]

A simplex in \(\mathbb R^4\) has volume

\[
\frac1{4!}\left|\det
\begin{pmatrix}
1&x_0\\
1&x_1\\
1&x_2\\
1&x_3\\
1&x_4
\end{pmatrix}\right|,
\]

where \(x_i\in\mathbb R^4\) are its vertices. Since volume is affine in each vertex separately, the maximum over \(K^5\) occurs when all vertices are extreme points of \(K\), hence on the moment curve. So write the vertices as

\[
p(t_i)=(t_i,t_i^2,t_i^3,t_i^4),\qquad 0\le t_i\le 1.
\]

Then

\[
\operatorname{Vol}
=\frac1{24}\left|\det
\begin{pmatrix}
1&t_0&t_0^2&t_0^3&t_0^4\\
1&t_1&t_1^2&t_1^3&t_1^4\\
1&t_2&t_2^2&t_2^3&t_2^4\\
1&t_3&t_3^2&t_3^3&t_3^4\\
1&t_4&t_4^2&t_4^3&t_4^4
\end{pmatrix}\right|
=\frac1{24}\prod_{i<j}|t_j-t_i|.
\]

Thus we must maximize the Vandermonde product for five points in \([0,1]\).

Rescale to \([-1,1]\) by \(t=(x+1)/2\). There are \(\binom52=10\) differences, so

\[
\prod_{i<j}|t_j-t_i|=2^{-10}\prod_{i<j}|x_j-x_i|.
\]

By symmetry, the maximizing five points on \([-1,1]\) are

\[
-1,\ -a,\ 0,\ a,\ 1.
\]

Their Vandermonde product is

\[
P(a)=4a^3(1-a^2)^2.
\]

Maximize:

\[
\frac{d}{da}\log P(a)
=\frac3a-\frac{4a}{1-a^2}=0,
\]

so

\[
3(1-a^2)=4a^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a^2=\frac37.
\]

Hence

\[
P_{\max}
=4\left(\frac37\right)^{3/2}\left(1-\frac37\right)^2
=4\cdot \frac{3\sqrt3}{7\sqrt7}\cdot \frac{16}{49}
=\frac{192\sqrt{21}}{343}.
\]

Returning to \([0,1]\),

\[
\prod_{i<j}|t_j-t_i|
=2^{-10}\cdot \frac{192\sqrt{21}}{343}.
\]

Therefore the maximum simplex volume is

\[
\frac1{24}\cdot 2^{-10}\cdot \frac{192\sqrt{21}}{343}
=\frac{8\sqrt{21}}{343\cdot 1024}
=\boxed{\frac{\sqrt{21}}{43904}}.
\]

So the exact maximum possible \(4\)-dimensional Euclidean volume is

\[
\boxed{\frac{\sqrt{21}}{43904}}.
\]
